paper.title: New Constant-gm circuit for precision chopper offset-stabilized operational amplifiers
paper.abstract: The paper presents a low-voltage chopper offset-stabilized operational amplifier with a new constant-gm technique, having a 1.8–5.5 V supply range, designed and simulated in a 0.25 µm CMOS process. The amplifier has an offset voltage of ±5 µV, minimum CMRR of 106 dB, minimum PSRR of 121 dB, 51 nV/√Hz voltage noise density and 550 kHz unity-gain bandwidth. The quiescent current is only 36 µA and was obtained due to the new low current constant-gm technique, which provides a variation of only 4% of the input transconductance and almost constant unity-gain bandwidth within the common-mode voltage range.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

verdict.summary: Simulated constant-gm input stage for a chopper op-amp: proportionate textbook formalism, low and relevant self-citation, thorough Monte Carlo and PVT evidence, but no silicon measurement and no released design files.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** A rail-to-rail CMOS input stage with a new constant-gm biasing scheme (dummy differential pairs plus current mirrors that inject a scaled current into the active pair and subtract it again at the outputs), integrated into a chopper offset-stabilized operational amplifier in a 0.25 µm process and evaluated by simulation.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** The contribution is a circuit-level refinement of a known approach (constant-gm by saturation control with dummy pairs), aimed at lower current consumption and constant output currents. It is assessed by circuit and Monte Carlo simulation. There is no new analytical model, no algorithm and no proof; an improvement of an existing method in a known design space is Level 2.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 (with constraints: 0)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 3 (weak-inversion transconductance gm = I/(nVth) in the three common-mode regions)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate — the three equations are the standard subthreshold transconductance relations that explain why the sum of tail currents must be held constant across the common-mode range. They carry the design argument of Sections 2 and 3, and the proposed circuit is then described against them ("Thus total transconductance is same as (1)"). They pass the necessity test.

### Issues
None identified in the formalism. The claim of an eightfold current saving rests on the Iref/8 mirror ratio stated in prose rather than on a worked current budget, but this is a presentation weakness, not decorative notation.

---

## Citation Analysis

14 references, 2 self-citations (SCR 14.3%). [1] is the authors' own CAS 2020 conference paper, of which the article is declared an extended version; [8] (Stănescu et al., CAS 2014) describes the passive RC notch filter used in the amplifier. Both are directly relevant (similarity well above 0.5).

Reference hygiene is weak. [4] and [6] are the same PACET 2017 paper listed twice under different numbers, and the text uses it both as the source of the saturation-control technique and as an example of methods "not suitable for precision operational amplifiers". The constant-sum-of-tail-currents technique is attributed to [2, 3], although [3] is a 28 nm chopper instrumentation-amplifier paper rather than a source for that technique. No citation-manipulation pattern is present.

---

## Structural Analysis

Claims are backed by extensive simulation evidence: frequency response, unity-gain bandwidth, phase margin and quiescent current versus common-mode voltage with and without the constant-gm circuit (Table 1); Monte Carlo offset and CMRR (Tables 2, 4, 5); transconductance spread under process variation (Fig. 10); PSRR and open-loop gain over supply and temperature (Tables 6, 7); noise, settling and slew-rate plots; and a comparison with two published chopper amplifiers (Table 8). The claim-evidence ratio is well above 1. All results are simulated; no measured silicon is reported, which the abstract states plainly ("designed and simulated").

Limitations are acknowledged inline: the proposed circuit is slower and more complex than the related-art techniques, and chopper stabilization degrades settling time, slew rate and step response. A small inconsistency between abstract and body (550 kHz versus 558 kHz unity-gain bandwidth) does not affect the conclusions.

No netlist, schematic file, simulation deck or result data is offered; the paper contains no availability statement or link.

---

## Conclusion

A competent analog-design paper with proportionate formalism: three textbook equations motivate a circuit modification whose benefit is demonstrated through a broad set of simulations, including Monte Carlo and PVT corners. Self-citation is low and relevant. The weaknesses are the absence of measured silicon, a duplicated and partly misattributed reference list, and no released design artifacts.

paper.title: Microheater optimized for the integration with metasurface-based IR sources for gas sensing application
paper.abstract: This paper presents the design, manufacturing stages, electrothermal analysis and characterization of micro-heaters with platinum (Pt) resistive layer in four geometric configurations, which can be integrated with metasurfaces absorbers with applications in gas detection. The results obtained according to the electrothermal analysis and the performed experiments show that the studied micro-heaters can be integrated with metasurfaces to obtain the IR emission, necessary for gas detection.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

verdict.summary: Pt meander microheaters designed in COMSOL, fabricated and characterised; textbook heat-transfer equations (with some errors) are proportionate, self-citation is low, but the claimed metasurface integration is not demonstrated and nothing is released.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Design by COMSOL electro-thermal simulation, fabrication and characterisation of four platinum meander microheaters on fused silica, intended to serve both as the broadband heat source and as the metal back-plane of a metasurface narrow-band IR emitter for CO2 sensing.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** Applied device engineering: a thin-film resistive heater laid out in four geometries, simulated with a commercial finite-element tool and measured with a thermocouple and an IR camera. No new model, algorithm or theory is proposed.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 (with constraints: 0)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 9 (Joule power, resistance of the film, generated heat, steady-state energy balance, conduction, convection, radiation, combined balance)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate — the equations are textbook heat-transfer relations, attributed to [15] and presented as the physics behind the COMSOL model. They are not used to compute any design value in the paper (the simulator does that), so they act as background rather than working formalism, but basic governing equations are within what Level 2 allows, and none of the theater patterns (set notation for collections, tuple definitions, decorative symbols for configuration constants) occurs. No necessity-test failure is recorded.

### Issues
The formulation contains correctness slips: the radiative loss is written as AR·ε·σ·ΔT^4, where the physics requires the difference of the fourth powers of absolute temperatures, and the Stefan-Boltzmann constant is given in W m^-2 °C^-4 instead of K^-4. Table 1 gives electrical conductivity in kg/m^3. These are errors, not theater; they remove any quality bonus.

---

## Citation Analysis

18 references, 2 self-citations (SCR 11.1%): [13] Tomescu et al. (META 2019) on controlling IR emissivity with metasurfaces, co-authored by R. Tomescu, and [14] Paun et al. (CAS 2020), the conference paper this work is declared to follow up. Both are directly relevant. The remaining references are reviews and primary work on NDIR gas sensing, metasurface absorbers and microheaters. No issues identified.

---

## Structural Analysis

Simulated temperature profiles (Fig. 4-8) and measurements (resistance versus temperature, thermocouple and IR-camera temperatures, transient response; Fig. 10-13) support the central result that all four heaters reach the 300 °C target below 20 V, and Fig. 12 shows measured and simulated temperatures in agreement. The stated novelty, however, is using the heater as the metasurface back-plane and improving heat transfer through an amorphous-silicon layer; neither is tested here, since no metasurface is integrated or optically characterised and no emission spectrum is reported. The abstract's conclusion that the heaters "can be integrated with metasurfaces to obtain the IR emission" therefore outruns the evidence. Uniformity is described only qualitatively ("rather good"). Claim-evidence balance is adequate overall (CER roughly 0.7).

Limitations are acknowledged inline: the 1 cm^2 active area is imposed by the existing test set-up and must be reduced to cut power consumption, and further miniaturisation is announced. No layout, simulation model or measurement data is offered; there is no availability statement or link.

---

## Conclusion

A sound but incremental device-engineering report. The heaters are well characterised and simulation agrees with measurement, and the formalism is proportionate textbook physics, marred by a few errors in the radiation term and units. The paper's own novelty claim, the integrated heater-as-back-plane emitter, awaits demonstration, and no artifacts are released.

paper.title: Manipulation of particles using dielectrophoresis in a microchannel
paper.abstract: Over the years several methods were used to separate cells within a microfluidic device such as cavities, with vortex microfluidics method, or cell trapping mechanisms using size filters. However, one of the methods that is widely used to separate cancer cells from blood cells is the dielectrophoresis. In this work we employ the numerical code COMSOL Multiphysics for a dielectrophoretic separation of CTCs (circulating tumor cells) from RBCs (red blood cells) in a 3D microchannel. The microfluidic device is composed of one inlet and three outlets. The non-uniform alternative electric field is generated using interdigitated electrodes and it separates the cells within the device to the corresponding outlet. The electric field frequency was set to 100 kHz. For this paper, one single CTC line is selected MDA-MB-231, breast cancer cells. The CTCs and the RBCs are considered in an ideal way in the simulation as spheres, but with the afferent characteristics. This work can be extended to testing multiple CTC lines at various flow velocities and electric field frequencies

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

verdict.summary: COMSOL study of dielectrophoretic CTC/RBC separation with a fabricated device and µPIV flow validation; standard physics equations are proportionate, self-citation is elevated but relevant, separation results are numerical only and nothing is released.

papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Numerical simulation in COMSOL of dielectrophoretic separation of circulating tumour cells (MDA-MB-231) from red blood cells in a microchannel with interdigitated electrodes, together with fabrication of the device and µPIV validation of the simulated flow field.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** Standard dielectrophoresis theory and a commercial multiphysics solver applied to a specific separation geometry. No new model or method is proposed; the work is an application study.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 (with constraints: 0)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 14 (DEP force, Clausius-Mossotti factor, complex permittivities, Reynolds number, hydraulic diameter, Stokes and continuity equations, quasi-static current equations, Newton's second law, Stokes drag)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate — the equations are the standard physics that specifies the three coupled simulation steps (laminar flow, electric currents, particle tracing), and the Clausius-Mossotti factor is used to interpret the frequency-dependent sign of the force (Fig. 6b). They pass the necessity test.

### Issues
No theater. Minor errors: the Stokes drag is written with an undefined V (presumably the relative particle velocity); the inlet velocity is given as "500 m/s" where µm/s is meant; and the text for Fig. 8a says both particles undergo negative dielectrophoresis yet "remain attached to the electrodes", which contradicts the mechanism the paper itself describes (negative DEP drives particles away from high field gradients).

---

## Citation Analysis

11 references, 2 self-citations (SCR 18.2%, elevated band but below the 20% flag threshold). [8] Chiriac, Avram and Bălan (CAS 2020) is the direct predecessor of this work (similarity about 0.9). [4] Avram A. et al. on a bipolar magnetophoretic system is co-authored by M. Avram and is cited as an example of active particle manipulation with magnetic fields; it is related (similarity about 0.5). Reference [1] lacks a venue, and [11] is the COMSOL manual. No concerning pattern.

---

## Structural Analysis

The flow simulation is checked against µPIV measurements on the fabricated device (Fig. 6a); the separation itself is shown only numerically, for one particle of each type and two frequencies (Fig. 8). The conclusion that high frequency separates the cells while 100 kHz does not follows from these figures. The abstract, however, states that "The electric field frequency was set to 100 kHz", the case in which separation fails, without mentioning that separation was obtained only at 4.5·10^8 Hz. CER is adequate.

Limitations are acknowledged inline: cells are idealised as spheres, the separating frequency "cannot really be obtained experimentally" without expensive equipment and may damage cells, and low velocities lead to clogging. No simulation model, geometry or data is offered; there is no availability statement or link.

---

## Conclusion

A modest application study with proportionate, standard formalism and an honest account of its practical limits. The experimental part validates only the flow field, the separation result rests on a two-particle simulation at an impractical frequency, and a few physical and numerical slips weaken the text. Self-citation is elevated but topically justified; no artifacts are released.

paper.title: Fabrication of Fresnel lenses operating as image correcting optical components for long infrared imaging systems
paper.abstract: We present the technological processes required to fabricate silicon Fresnel lenses with sixteen discrete depth levels operating as corrector optical components for long infrared imaging systems. In order to configure the discrete surface of the lenses, four separated photolithographic processes each one of them followed by deep reactive ion etching were used. In order to detach the configured lenses presenting a disk like shape from the wafer, a DRIE Bosch deep etching process was employed. Finally, an antireflective layer consisting of a nanostructured surface was configured on both sides of the lenses in order to improve the transmission in LWIR spectral range. The geometrical parameters of the fabricated Fresnel lenses were determined by white light interferometry method and it was found that they are in good agreement with the design specifications. The optical and scanning electron microscopy measurements reveal a high quality of the optical surface with a low value of roughness. The spectral characteristics of the lenses in the LWIR spectral region reveal a transmission of above 70%.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

flag_details.NO_LIMITATIONS: No limitations section and no inline acknowledgment of the work's own constraints: the only drawbacks discussed belong to competing approaches (metasurfaces, bulk Fresnel lenses). Process tolerances, surface roughness, yield and the absence of any optical imaging or aberration-correction test are not acknowledged.

verdict.summary: Process description for 16-level silicon LWIR Fresnel lenses with WLI and FTIR characterisation; minimal, necessary formalism and low relevant self-citation, but the image-correcting function is never tested, limitations are not discussed, and nothing is released.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** The process flow for 16-level silicon Fresnel corrector lenses for long-wave infrared: four photolithography steps each followed by cryogenic DRIE, through-wafer Bosch release, KOH back-thinning and metal-assisted chemical etching of antireflective nanostructures, characterised by white-light interferometry, optical and SEM microscopy and FTIR transmission.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** A fabrication report combining established microfabrication techniques (binary multilevel lithography, cryogenic and Bosch DRIE, KOH, MACE) to produce a known optical element. No new theory or design method is proposed.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 (with constraints: 0)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 1 inline design relation, d = λ/(n − 1), plus the binary depth partition d/2, d/4, d/8 stated inline

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate — the single relation fixes the 2π step height (3.93 µm at 9.5 µm) and the binary partition fixes the four etch depths actually used. Both are needed to reproduce the process and pass the necessity test.

### Issues
None identified.

---

## Citation Analysis

20 references, 2 self-citations (SCR 10%): [14] Rebigan et al. (CAS 2020), the conference version from which Figs. 1 and 2 are reproduced with attribution, and [19] Rebigan et al. (JOAM 2020) on the nanostructured antireflective layers, to which the details of that step are deferred. Both are directly relevant.

There are citation errors that are not manipulation: the silicon refractive index is attributed to [10] (a paper on an infrared camera), while [20] (Salzberg and Villa, infrared refractive indexes of silicon) is never cited in the text; [5] appears only through the range "[4, 6]". [15] is a vendor web page for a cryogenic etch process.

---

## Structural Analysis

The process claims are supported: etch parameters are tabulated (Tables 1, 2), WLI cross-sections show step heights of about 250 nm as designed (Fig. 9), and FTIR spectra show transmission above 70% for the thinned, antireflection-treated lens (Fig. 7). Two claims outrun the evidence. The abstract asserts "a low value of roughness", but no roughness value is reported. The title and abstract describe the lenses as "operating as image correcting optical components", yet no imaging, focal-length or aberration measurement is presented; the optical function is inferred from the geometry alone. The text also contains unit errors (lens thicknesses given as 270 nm and 540 nm where 270 µm and about 530 µm are meant). CER is adequate overall.

No limitations of the work are acknowledged (see flag). No mask layouts, process files or measurement data are offered; the only URL in the paper is a third-party vendor page, which is not an artifact of the authors.

---

## Conclusion

A clear, practically useful process description with minimal and necessary formalism and low, relevant self-citation. Its weaknesses are structural: the optical function named in the title is never tested, surface quality is asserted without numbers, limitations are absent, and several citation and unit errors remain. No artifacts are released.

paper.title: Investigations of the Fabricated Nothing On Insulator Nanodevices as Metal-Air-Metal variant - NOI-MAM
paper.abstract: This paper presents some investigations of an experimental Nothing On Insulator device, made in the Metal-Air-Metal (NOI-MAM) variant. The vacuum nanodevices are potential candidates for tera-Hertz applications. The investigations concern the fabrication processes, measurements of the output characteristics and simulations of the NOI-MAM devices. Two metallic nanowires are considered instead of two semiconductor nano-islands for Source and Drain. Air molecules in normal conditions inside a gap of maximum 36 nm size represents the "Nothing" area. The electron-beam lithography technology or AFM sectioning by tips are investigated by SEM and AFM analysis. The measured and simulated current-voltage curves are investigated for potential applications.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

Ravariu, including a Romanian patent [10]); [16]-[18], [21] (Ravariu with co-authors Manea, Parvulescu, Dinescu, Gavrila, Purica, Srinivasulu); [29] (co-author Srinivasulu). papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Fabrication of Cr/Au nanowire pairs separated by 19-31 nm air gaps (by electron-beam lithography and lift-off, and alternatively by AFM-tip scratching) forming a "Nothing On Insulator" metal-air-metal device, with current-voltage measurements and Atlas/Silvaco simulation of electric field, lattice temperature and I-V curves.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** Experimental nanofabrication and characterisation, complemented by simulation in a commercial device simulator with built-in models (MIM tunnelling, lattice heating). No new physical model, algorithm or proof is developed.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 (with constraints: 0)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 0

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate — there is no formal apparatus at all. If anything the paper errs the other way: the conduction mechanism (MIM tunnelling) and the maximum dissipated powers (105-222 nW) are asserted without any expression or derivation, so a reader cannot check them.

### Issues
None identified in the formalism.

---

## Citation Analysis

29 references, 13 self-citations (SCR 44.8%), above the 30% threshold (see flag). Eight are sole-authored by the first author ([4], [9]-[13], [15], [19], one of them a patent), four are co-authored with the present team ([16]-[18], [21]), and one is by co-author Srinivasulu ([29]). The text itself remarks that "some authors who cited our previous work [12]" reported a related device. Most self-citations are on-topic: they trace the NOI device from proposal through simulation to the 2020 fabrication. [29] (ULPD and CPTL pull-up stages for DCVSL) is marginal; it supports a tacked-on paragraph proposing a logic-circuit application that the paper never investigates.

A non-self anomaly: [20], a paper on chitosan as a biomedical material, is cited within "separate simulations [18-21]" of NOI-MAM devices, and has no evident connection to the topic. Whether it reflects a reciprocal arrangement cannot be established from this paper alone, so no CITATION_RING_INDICATOR is raised, but the citation is unexplained.

---

## Structural Analysis

The fabrication claims are supported by SEM images and the gap sizes in Fig. 2, and measured I-V curves are shown for NOI1/NOI2 (Fig. 6) and NOI3 (Fig. 7, compared against points picked from three published devices). Several claims lack shown evidence: "As experimental measurements predicted, the Drain-Source electrodes heating occurs at VDS = 50 V up to 1000 K", though no thermal measurement is reported; the maximum power limits are stated as results of material constants from [28] without the calculation; the equivalence of the air gap to vacuum rests on a single mean-free-path argument; and the conclusion that the simulations "indicated possible applications in Differential Cascode Voltage Switch Logic" has no circuit simulation behind it. CER is weak, around 0.45.

Limitations are acknowledged inline: AFM scratching did not fully separate the nanowires, gate modulation is absent, and simulated and measured I-V curves differ. No layout, simulation input deck or measured data is offered; there is no availability statement or link.

---

## Conclusion

An exploratory device paper with no formal apparatus and honest acknowledgment of several negative results, but with weak support for its application claims. The decisive problem is citation conduct: 13 of 29 references are the authors' own, together with an unexplained off-topic citation, which triggers the disqualifying self-citation flag. No artifacts are released.
